Arnold of Soissons (Arnoul) was a 11th-century saint of the Catholic Church, serving as a bishop and later being canonized as a saint. He played a significant role in the establishment of the Catholic Church in the region, particularly in the area now known as Belgium. Through his religious leadership and charitable work, Arnold of Soissons left a lasting legacy as the patron saint of hop-pickers and Belgian brewers.

Born in the 11th century, Arnold's life is shrouded in mystery, with few historical records available. However, it is known that he rose to prominence as a cleric and eventually became the bishop of Soissons. His influence extended beyond his diocese, as he participated in several ecumenical councils and was involved in the translation of liturgical texts.

Arnold of Soissons' legacy can be seen in the many institutions and charities he founded, including a hospital and a school for the poor. His feast day, celebrated on June 9, is still observed by the Catholic Church today.

The saint's significance can be measured by his impact on the religious landscape of Europe during the Middle Ages. His work in establishing the Catholic Church in the region helped shape the spiritual identity of the people, and his charitable efforts left a lasting impact on the community.
